title: Canvas 2D Isometric Rendering Research
summary: Practical Canvas 2D patterns for Bobby. Sprite sheets, Z-sorting, camera pan/zoom, click detection, React integration. Code-ready.
content:
Canvas 2D Isometric Rendering Research

Steffen | 2026-03-16 For Bobby. Practical code patterns, not theory. Copy-paste into Corner when you're ready for Phase 2.

Why Canvas (Not DOM/SVG)

Bobby's current Phase 1 approach (single background image + DOM overlays) works. When Phase 2 hits (dynamic rooms, furniture placement, marketplace, style packs), we need Canvas because:

  • DOM reflows kill performance when you have 100+ individual furniture sprites animating
  • Canvas draws 500+ sprites at 60fps without breaking a sweat
  • Pixel-perfect rendering with imageSmoothingEnabled = false (critical for our pixel art)
  • Camera transforms (pan/zoom) are a single ctx.setTransform() call, not CSS on 100 elements
  • Hit detection is math, not event bubbling through overlapping divs

When to switch: Not yet. Phase 1 works. Switch when dynamic room rendering or the furniture marketplace demands it. This doc is the blueprint so the switch is painless.

1. Sprite Sheets vs Individual PNGs

Verdict: Sprite sheets. Always.

Individual PNGs mean one HTTP request and one Image object per frame per agent per state. For 13 agents with 4 states averaging 5 frames each, that's 260 separate image loads. Sprite sheets collapse that to 13-52 files.

But the real win is draw performance. drawImage() with a sprite sheet uses source-rect clipping to grab the right frame. The GPU keeps one texture in memory instead of swapping between hundreds.

Sprite Sheet Format (Matching c2-sprite-spec.md)

Two formats work. Pick one per project and stick with it.

Option A: One sheet per state (current spec)

sprites/patrik/idle.png     -> 128x32 (4 frames x 32px)
sprites/patrik/thinking.png -> 192x32 (6 frames x 32px)
sprites/patrik/speaking.png -> 128x32 (4 frames x 32px)
sprites/patrik/done.png     -> 192x32 (6 frames x 32px)

Option B: One sheet per agent (more efficient)

sprites/patrik-all.png -> 256x128 (8 cols x 4 rows, padded to max frames)

Row 0 = idle (4 frames), Row 1 = thinking (6 frames), Row 2 = speaking (4 frames), Row 3 = done (6 frames). Empty cells are transparent.

Option B is better for Canvas. Fewer image objects, fewer texture swaps.

Loading Pattern

interface SpriteSheet {
  image: HTMLImageElement;
  frameWidth: number;
  frameHeight: number;
  states: Record<string, { row: number; frameCount: number; frameDuration: number }>;
}

async function loadSpriteSheet(agentId: string): Promise<SpriteSheet> {
  const img = new Image();
  img.src = `/sprites/${agentId}-all.png`;
  await new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    img.onload = resolve;
    img.onerror = reject;
  });

  return {
    image: img,
    frameWidth: 32,  // or 64 for detail view
    frameHeight: 32,
    states: {
      idle:     { row: 0, frameCount: 4, frameDuration: 800 },
      thinking: { row: 1, frameCount: 6, frameDuration: 400 },
      speaking: { row: 2, frameCount: 4, frameDuration: 200 },
      done:     { row: 3, frameCount: 6, frameDuration: 300 },
    },
  };
}

Drawing a Frame

function drawSprite(
  ctx: CanvasRenderingContext2D,
  sheet: SpriteSheet,
  state: string,
  frameIndex: number,
  x: number,
  y: number,
  scale: number = 1
) {
  const stateInfo = sheet.states[state];
  if (!stateInfo) return;

  const frame = frameIndex % stateInfo.frameCount;
  const sx = frame * sheet.frameWidth;
  const sy = stateInfo.row * sheet.frameHeight;

  // Critical for pixel art: disable smoothing
  ctx.imageSmoothingEnabled = false;

  ctx.drawImage(
    sheet.image,
    sx, sy, sheet.frameWidth, sheet.frameHeight,           // source rect
    x, y, sheet.frameWidth * scale, sheet.frameHeight * scale // dest rect
  );
}

Animation Timing

Don't tie frame advancement to requestAnimationFrame directly. Use elapsed time so animations stay correct even if the frame rate drops.

class SpriteAnimator {
  private elapsed = 0;
  private currentFrame = 0;

  update(deltaMs: number, frameDuration: number, frameCount: number): number {
    this.elapsed += deltaMs;
    if (this.elapsed >= frameDuration) {
      this.elapsed -= frameDuration;
      this.currentFrame = (this.currentFrame + 1) % frameCount;
    }
    return this.currentFrame;
  }

  reset() {
    this.elapsed = 0;
    this.currentFrame = 0;
  }
}

Preloading All Sheets

Load everything before the first render. No pop-in.

async function preloadAllSprites(agentIds: string[]): Promise<Map<string, SpriteSheet>> {
  const sheets = new Map<string, SpriteSheet>();
  const promises = agentIds.map(async (id) => {
    const sheet = await loadSpriteSheet(id);
    sheets.set(id, sheet);
  });
  await Promise.all(promises);
  return sheets;
}

Walking Sprite Sheets (c3-walking-sprites-spec.md)

Walking sheets follow the same pattern but with direction as the row key:

walkStates: {
  'walk-ne': { row: 0, frameCount: 6, frameDuration: 150 },
  'walk-nw': { row: 1, frameCount: 6, frameDuration: 150 },
  'walk-se': { row: 2, frameCount: 6, frameDuration: 150 },
  'walk-sw': { row: 3, frameCount: 6, frameDuration: 150 },
}

Use a separate sheet file (patrik-walk.png) or extend the main sheet with additional rows. Separate files are simpler for asset pipeline management.

2. Z-Sorting (Painter's Algorithm, Y-Sort)

The Problem

Isometric has no real depth buffer. Objects further from the camera need to draw first so closer objects paint over them. Without sorting, a character behind a desk might render in front of it.

Solution: Y-Sort (Isometric Standard)

In a 2:1 isometric view, the Y coordinate in world space directly maps to draw order. Higher Y = closer to camera = drawn later (on top).

interface Drawable {
  worldX: number;   // isometric world position
  worldY: number;
  zLayer: number;   // base layer (floor=0, furniture=1, character=2, effects=3)
  draw(ctx: CanvasRenderingContext2D): void;
}

function sortDrawables(items: Drawable[]): Drawable[] {
  return items.sort((a, b) => {
    // Primary sort: layer (floors before furniture before characters)
    if (a.zLayer !== b.zLayer) return a.zLayer - b.zLayer;
    // Secondary sort: Y position (back-to-front)
    if (a.worldY !== b.worldY) return a.worldY - b.worldY;
    // Tertiary sort: X position (left-to-right for ties)
    return a.worldX - b.worldX;
  });
}

Layer System (Matching compositing-spec.md)

Map the 7-layer compositing stack to zLayer values:

Compositing Layer zLayer Contents
Void Background (L1) N/A CSS, not Canvas
Ground Plane (L2) 0 Dark surface, light pools
Building Shell (L3) 1 Walls, roof, CORNER sign
Room Interiors (L4) 2 Floors, then furniture
Character Sprites (L5) 3 Agents at desks or walking
Light Overlays (L6) 4 Window glow, agent glow
UI Elements (L7) N/A DOM overlay (HUD, chat)

Layers 1 and 7 stay in DOM. Layers 2-6 render on Canvas. This hybrid approach gives us Canvas performance for the game world and DOM flexibility for the HUD.

Room-Level Optimization

Don't Y-sort the entire scene every frame. Sort within rooms.

interface Room {
  id: string;
  baseY: number;          // room's Y position in world space
  drawables: Drawable[];  // furniture + character for this room
}

function renderScene(ctx: CanvasRenderingContext2D, rooms: Room[]) {
  // Sort rooms by Y (back to front)
  const sortedRooms = [...rooms].sort((a, b) => a.baseY - b.baseY);

  for (const room of sortedRooms) {
    // Sort items within each room
    const sorted = sortDrawables(room.drawables);
    for (const item of sorted) {
      item.draw(ctx);
    }
  }
}

For Corner's 14-room layout, this means sorting ~8-12 items per room instead of 100+ items globally. Faster and more predictable.

Isometric Coordinate Conversion

Bobby needs these constantly. World space (grid) to screen space (pixels) and back.

const TILE_WIDTH = 64;   // from c2-grid-spec.json cellSize
const TILE_HEIGHT = 32;  // 2:1 ratio (isoRatio from spec)

// World grid (col, row) to screen pixel (x, y)
function worldToScreen(col: number, row: number): { x: number; y: number } {
  return {
    x: (col - row) * (TILE_WIDTH / 2),
    y: (col + row) * (TILE_HEIGHT / 2),
  };
}

// Screen pixel to world grid (inverse)
function screenToWorld(screenX: number, screenY: number): { col: number; row: number } {
  return {
    col: (screenX / (TILE_WIDTH / 2) + screenY / (TILE_HEIGHT / 2)) / 2,
    row: (screenY / (TILE_HEIGHT / 2) - screenX / (TILE_WIDTH / 2)) / 2,
  };
}

These functions are the bridge between click events (screen space) and the game grid (world space).

3. Camera Pan/Zoom on Canvas

How It Works

Instead of moving every object, move the "camera" by applying a transform matrix to the entire Canvas context. Every drawImage and fillRect call automatically renders at the transformed position.

interface Camera {
  x: number;       // camera position in world space
  y: number;
  zoom: number;    // 0.5 (overview) to 3.5 (room detail), from c3-room-zoom-spec.md
  targetX: number; // for smooth transitions
  targetY: number;
  targetZoom: number;
}

function applyCamera(ctx: CanvasRenderingContext2D, camera: Camera, canvas: HTMLCanvasElement) {
  ctx.setTransform(
    camera.zoom, 0,
    0, camera.zoom,
    -camera.x * camera.zoom + canvas.width / 2,
    -camera.y * camera.zoom + canvas.height / 2
  );
}

This single call handles ALL pan and zoom behavior. Every draw call after it is automatically positioned.

Smooth Camera Transitions (Matching Room Zoom Spec)

The room zoom spec defines cubic-bezier curves for zoom transitions. Implement with lerp + easing:

function easeOutQuint(t: number): number {
  // Approximates cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.9, 0.3, 1.0) from the zoom spec
  return 1 - Math.pow(1 - t, 5);
}

function easeInOutCubic(t: number): number {
  // For the "helicopter pullback" (L3 to L1)
  return t < 0.5 ? 4 * t * t * t : 1 - Math.pow(-2 * t + 2, 3) / 2;
}

class SmoothCamera {
  private startX = 0;
  private startY = 0;
  private startZoom = 1;
  private progress = 0;
  private duration = 0;
  private easing: (t: number) => number = easeOutQuint;

  camera: Camera = { x: 0, y: 0, zoom: 0.7, targetX: 0, targetY: 0, targetZoom: 0.7 };

  // Trigger a zoom transition (called on room click)
  zoomTo(x: number, y: number, zoom: number, durationMs: number, easing?: (t: number) => number) {
    this.startX = this.camera.x;
    this.startY = this.camera.y;
    this.startZoom = this.camera.zoom;
    this.camera.targetX = x;
    this.camera.targetY = y;
    this.camera.targetZoom = zoom;
    this.duration = durationMs;
    this.progress = 0;
    if (easing) this.easing = easing;
  }

  update(deltaMs: number) {
    if (this.progress >= 1) return;

    this.progress = Math.min(1, this.progress + deltaMs / this.duration);
    const t = this.easing(this.progress);

    this.camera.x = this.startX + (this.camera.targetX - this.startX) * t;
    this.camera.y = this.startY + (this.camera.targetY - this.startY) * t;
    this.camera.zoom = this.startZoom + (this.camera.targetZoom - this.startZoom) * t;
  }
}

Zoom Level Transitions (from c3-room-zoom-spec.md)

// Room zoom transitions mapped to spec
const ZOOM_TRANSITIONS = {
  overviewToNeighborhood: { zoom: 1.6, duration: 400, easing: easeOutQuint },
  neighborhoodToDetail:   { zoom: 2.8, duration: 350, easing: easeOutQuint },
  detailToOverview:       { zoom: 0.7, duration: 500, easing: easeInOutCubic },
  roomToRoom:             { duration: 600, easing: easeInOutCubic },  // zoom stays 1.6
};

function onRoomClick(roomId: string, camera: SmoothCamera, rooms: Room[]) {
  const room = rooms.find(r => r.id === roomId);
  if (!room) return;

  const screenPos = worldToScreen(room.position.col, room.position.row);
  const currentZoom = camera.camera.zoom;

  if (currentZoom < 1.0) {
    // Overview to Neighborhood
    camera.zoomTo(screenPos.x, screenPos.y, 1.6, 400);
  } else if (currentZoom < 2.2) {
    // Room to Room pan (stay at 1.6x)
    camera.zoomTo(screenPos.x, screenPos.y, 1.6, 600, easeInOutCubic);
  }
}

Scroll Wheel Zoom

function handleWheel(e: WheelEvent, camera: SmoothCamera, canvas: HTMLCanvasElement) {
  e.preventDefault();

  const zoomSensitivity = 0.15;  // from room zoom spec
  const minZoom = 0.5;
  const maxZoom = 3.5;

  const delta = e.deltaY > 0 ? -zoomSensitivity : zoomSensitivity;
  const newZoom = Math.max(minZoom, Math.min(maxZoom, camera.camera.zoom + delta));

  // Zoom toward mouse position (not center)
  const rect = canvas.getBoundingClientRect();
  const mouseX = e.clientX - rect.left;
  const mouseY = e.clientY - rect.top;

  // Convert mouse to world position before zoom
  const worldMouseX = (mouseX - canvas.width / 2) / camera.camera.zoom + camera.camera.x;
  const worldMouseY = (mouseY - canvas.height / 2) / camera.camera.zoom + camera.camera.y;

  // After zoom, the world position under the mouse should stay the same
  const newCamX = worldMouseX - (mouseX - canvas.width / 2) / newZoom;
  const newCamY = worldMouseY - (mouseY - canvas.height / 2) / newZoom;

  camera.zoomTo(newCamX, newCamY, newZoom, 200);  // 200ms ease-out per spec
}

Mouse Drag Pan with Momentum

class PanHandler {
  private isDragging = false;
  private lastX = 0;
  private lastY = 0;
  private velocityX = 0;
  private velocityY = 0;
  private friction = 0.92;  // from room zoom spec: multiply by 0.92 per frame

  onMouseDown(e: MouseEvent) {
    this.isDragging = true;
    this.lastX = e.clientX;
    this.lastY = e.clientY;
    this.velocityX = 0;
    this.velocityY = 0;
  }

  onMouseMove(e: MouseEvent, camera: Camera) {
    if (!this.isDragging) return;

    const dx = e.clientX - this.lastX;
    const dy = e.clientY - this.lastY;

    // Move camera opposite to drag direction, scaled by zoom
    camera.x -= dx / camera.zoom;
    camera.y -= dy / camera.zoom;

    this.velocityX = dx;
    this.velocityY = dy;
    this.lastX = e.clientX;
    this.lastY = e.clientY;
  }

  onMouseUp() {
    this.isDragging = false;
  }

  // Call every frame for momentum
  updateMomentum(camera: Camera) {
    if (this.isDragging) return;
    if (Math.abs(this.velocityX) < 0.5 && Math.abs(this.velocityY) < 0.5) return;

    camera.x -= this.velocityX / camera.zoom;
    camera.y -= this.velocityY / camera.zoom;

    this.velocityX *= this.friction;
    this.velocityY *= this.friction;
  }
}

Camera Bounds Clamping

function clampCamera(camera: Camera, worldWidth: number, worldHeight: number, canvasWidth: number, canvasHeight: number) {
  const padding = 0.2;  // 20% padding from room zoom spec
  const viewW = canvasWidth / camera.zoom;
  const viewH = canvasHeight / camera.zoom;

  const minX = -worldWidth * padding;
  const maxX = worldWidth * (1 + padding) - viewW;
  const minY = -worldHeight * padding;
  const maxY = worldHeight * (1 + padding) - viewH;

  camera.x = Math.max(minX, Math.min(maxX, camera.x));
  camera.y = Math.max(minY, Math.min(maxY, camera.y));
}

4. Click Detection on Canvas Sprites

Canvas doesn't have built-in event targets like DOM. Two approaches, from simple to advanced.

Approach A: Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB)

Fast, simple, good enough for 90% of cases. Each clickable object registers a rectangular hit area.

interface HitArea {
  id: string;           // room or agent ID
  x: number;            // world-space position
  y: number;
  width: number;
  height: number;
  onClick?: () => void;
  onHover?: () => void;
}

function hitTest(
  screenX: number,
  screenY: number,
  camera: Camera,
  canvas: HTMLCanvasElement,
  hitAreas: HitArea[]
): HitArea | null {
  // Convert screen coords to world coords
  const worldX = (screenX - canvas.width / 2) / camera.zoom + camera.x;
  const worldY = (screenY - canvas.height / 2) / camera.zoom + camera.y;

  // Test back-to-front (reverse draw order) so topmost wins
  for (let i = hitAreas.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
    const area = hitAreas[i];
    if (
      worldX >= area.x &&
      worldX <= area.x + area.width &&
      worldY >= area.y &&
      worldY <= area.y + area.height
    ) {
      return area;
    }
  }
  return null;
}

Approach B: Isometric Diamond Hit Test (for Tile/Room Clicks)

Rooms in isometric view are diamonds, not rectangles. AABB works if your rooms are always rectangular on screen. For proper isometric tile clicking:

function isInsideIsoDiamond(
  worldX: number,
  worldY: number,
  tileCol: number,
  tileRow: number,
  tileCols: number,  // room width in grid cells
  tileRows: number   // room height in grid cells
): boolean {
  // Get the room's center in screen space
  const centerCol = tileCol + tileCols / 2;
  const centerRow = tileRow + tileRows / 2;
  const center = worldToScreen(centerCol, centerRow);

  // The diamond half-widths
  const halfW = (tileCols * TILE_WIDTH) / 2;
  const halfH = (tileRows * TILE_HEIGHT) / 2;

  const clickScreen = worldToScreen(worldX, worldY);

  // Diamond test: |dx/halfW| + |dy/halfH| <= 1
  const dx = Math.abs(clickScreen.x - center.x) / halfW;
  const dy = Math.abs(clickScreen.y - center.y) / halfH;

  return (dx + dy) <= 1;
}

Approach C: Color-Picking (Pixel-Perfect, Advanced)

Render a hidden "ID canvas" where each clickable region is a unique solid color. On click, read the pixel color to identify the target. This is how professional 2D engines do it.

class HitCanvas {
  private canvas: HTMLCanvasElement;
  private ctx: CanvasRenderingContext2D;
  private colorMap = new Map<string, string>();  // color hex -> entity ID

  constructor(width: number, height: number) {
    this.canvas = document.createElement('canvas');
    this.canvas.width = width;
    this.canvas.height = height;
    this.ctx = this.canvas.getContext('2d')!;
  }

  // Assign a unique color to each entity
  registerEntity(id: string): string {
    // Generate unique color from entity index
    const index = this.colorMap.size + 1;
    const r = (index >> 16) & 0xFF;
    const g = (index >> 8) & 0xFF;
    const b = index & 0xFF;
    const color = `rgb(${r},${g},${b})`;
    this.colorMap.set(color, id);
    return color;
  }

  // Render hit areas as solid colored shapes (same positions as main canvas)
  renderHitArea(x: number, y: number, w: number, h: number, color: string) {
    this.ctx.fillStyle = color;
    this.ctx.fillRect(x, y, w, h);
  }

  // Check what was clicked
  getEntityAtPixel(x: number, y: number): string | null {
    const pixel = this.ctx.getImageData(x, y, 1, 1).data;
    const color = `rgb(${pixel[0]},${pixel[1]},${pixel[2]})`;
    return this.colorMap.get(color) ?? null;
  }

  // Apply same camera transform as main canvas
  applyCamera(camera: Camera) {
    this.ctx.setTransform(
      camera.zoom, 0, 0, camera.zoom,
      -camera.x * camera.zoom + this.canvas.width / 2,
      -camera.y * camera.zoom + this.canvas.height / 2
    );
  }

  clear() {
    this.ctx.setTransform(1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0);
    this.ctx.clearRect(0, 0, this.canvas.width, this.canvas.height);
  }
}

Recommendation for Corner

Start with AABB (Approach A). Bobby's current overlay system uses percentage-based rectangles. AABB is the direct Canvas equivalent. It handles room clicks, agent clicks, and furniture clicks well enough.

Add isometric diamond testing (Approach B) when tile-level precision matters (furniture marketplace, room editor).

Skip color-picking (Approach C) unless we need pixel-perfect hit testing on irregular shapes. It's overkill for Corner's room-based layout.

Hover State Handling

Canvas doesn't fire mouseenter/mouseleave. Track hover manually:

let hoveredEntity: string | null = null;

function onMouseMove(e: MouseEvent, camera: Camera, canvas: HTMLCanvasElement, hitAreas: HitArea[]) {
  const rect = canvas.getBoundingClientRect();
  const hit = hitTest(e.clientX - rect.left, e.clientY - rect.top, camera, canvas, hitAreas);
  const newHovered = hit?.id ?? null;

  if (newHovered !== hoveredEntity) {
    // Hover changed
    if (hoveredEntity) {
      // trigger "hover leave" on old entity
      canvas.style.cursor = 'default';
    }
    if (newHovered) {
      // trigger "hover enter" on new entity
      canvas.style.cursor = 'pointer';
    }
    hoveredEntity = newHovered;
  }
}

The room hover glow from c2-grid-spec.json (glowColor: agentColor, glowOpacity: 0.3) gets applied in the render loop based on hoveredEntity.

5. Canvas + React Integration

The Core Pattern: useRef + Imperative Draw Loop

React owns the component lifecycle. Canvas owns the rendering. They communicate through refs and state, never through re-renders.

import React, { useRef, useEffect, useCallback, useState } from 'react';

interface GameCanvasProps {
  agents: AgentState[];       // from your state management
  rooms: RoomData[];          // from c2-grid-spec.json
  selectedRoom: string | null;
}

function GameCanvas({ agents, rooms, selectedRoom }: GameCanvasProps) {
  const canvasRef = useRef<HTMLCanvasElement>(null);
  const animFrameRef = useRef<number>(0);
  const lastTimeRef = useRef<number>(0);
  const cameraRef = useRef(new SmoothCamera());
  const spritesRef = useRef<Map<string, SpriteSheet>>(new Map());

  // Stable references to props (avoid stale closures in the render loop)
  const agentsRef = useRef(agents);
  const roomsRef = useRef(rooms);
  useEffect(() => { agentsRef.current = agents; }, [agents]);
  useEffect(() => { roomsRef.current = rooms; }, [rooms]);

  // Load sprites once
  useEffect(() => {
    const agentIds = rooms.map(r => r.id).filter(Boolean);
    preloadAllSprites(agentIds).then(sheets => {
      spritesRef.current = sheets;
    });
  }, []); // intentional empty deps: load once

  // The render loop: completely outside React's render cycle
  const renderLoop = useCallback((timestamp: number) => {
    const canvas = canvasRef.current;
    if (!canvas) return;

    const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');
    if (!ctx) return;

    const delta = timestamp - lastTimeRef.current;
    lastTimeRef.current = timestamp;

    // Update camera
    cameraRef.current.update(delta);

    // Clear
    ctx.setTransform(1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0);
    ctx.clearRect(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);

    // Apply camera transform
    applyCamera(ctx, cameraRef.current.camera, canvas);

    // Draw scene (back to front)
    drawGroundPlane(ctx);
    drawBuildingShell(ctx);
    drawRooms(ctx, roomsRef.current, agentsRef.current, spritesRef.current, delta);
    drawLightOverlays(ctx, roomsRef.current);

    // Reset transform for any screen-space UI drawn on canvas
    ctx.setTransform(1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0);

    animFrameRef.current = requestAnimationFrame(renderLoop);
  }, []);

  // Start/stop the loop
  useEffect(() => {
    lastTimeRef.current = performance.now();
    animFrameRef.current = requestAnimationFrame(renderLoop);
    return () => cancelAnimationFrame(animFrameRef.current);
  }, [renderLoop]);

  // Handle canvas resize
  useEffect(() => {
    const canvas = canvasRef.current;
    if (!canvas) return;

    const resize = () => {
      const dpr = window.devicePixelRatio || 1;
      const parent = canvas.parentElement;
      if (!parent) return;

      canvas.width = parent.clientWidth * dpr;
      canvas.height = parent.clientHeight * dpr;
      canvas.style.width = `${parent.clientWidth}px`;
      canvas.style.height = `${parent.clientHeight}px`;

      const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');
      if (ctx) ctx.scale(dpr, dpr);
    };

    resize();
    const observer = new ResizeObserver(resize);
    observer.observe(canvas.parentElement!);
    return () => observer.disconnect();
  }, []);

  return (
    <div style={{ width: '100%', height: '100%', position: 'relative' }}>
      <canvas
        ref={canvasRef}
        style={{ display: 'block', width: '100%', height: '100%' }}
        onMouseDown={handleMouseDown}
        onMouseMove={handleMouseMove}
        onMouseUp={handleMouseUp}
        onWheel={handleWheel}
        onClick={handleClick}
      />
      {/* DOM-based HUD overlays go here as siblings */}
    </div>
  );
}

Critical Rules for Canvas + React

1. Never let React re-render trigger a canvas redraw. The requestAnimationFrame loop runs 60fps independently. React state changes update refs, not the canvas directly. This prevents React's reconciliation from interfering with smooth animation.

2. Use refs for everything the render loop reads. agentsRef.current, roomsRef.current, cameraRef.current. Direct ref reads in the loop avoid stale closure problems.

3. Handle DPR (Device Pixel Ratio). Retina displays need canvas.width = displayWidth * dpr with ctx.scale(dpr, dpr). Without this, everything looks blurry on MacBooks and phones.

4. Events go on the canvas element, not the window. Keyboard events are the exception (those go on window or a container div with tabIndex).

5. imageSmoothingEnabled = false on every frame. Canvas resets this property when resized. Set it at the start of every render pass. This is non-negotiable for pixel art.

// At the top of every render loop iteration:
ctx.imageSmoothingEnabled = false;

Hybrid Approach: Canvas Game + DOM HUD

This is what Corner should use. The isometric world renders on Canvas. The HUD, chat bar, menus, and panels are React DOM components positioned over the canvas with CSS.

function CornerApp() {
  const [selectedAgent, setSelectedAgent] = useState<string | null>(null);
  const [zoomLevel, setZoomLevel] = useState<'overview' | 'neighborhood' | 'detail'>('overview');

  return (
    <div className="corner-container" style={{ position: 'relative', width: '100vw', height: '100vh' }}>
      {/* Canvas layer: game world */}
      <GameCanvas
        agents={agents}
        rooms={rooms}
        selectedRoom={selectedAgent}
        onRoomClick={(roomId) => setSelectedAgent(roomId)}
        onZoomChange={(level) => setZoomLevel(level)}
      />

      {/* DOM layer: HUD (from hud-blue-spec.md) */}
      <HudBar zoomLevel={zoomLevel} />

      {/* DOM layer: Chat bar */}
      <ChatBar selectedAgent={selectedAgent} />

      {/* DOM layer: Side menu */}
      <SideMenu />

      {/* DOM layer: Mini-map (visible at zoom level 2+) */}
      {zoomLevel !== 'overview' && <MiniMap />}
    </div>
  );
}

Why hybrid?

  • Canvas: 60fps game rendering, camera transforms, sprite animation. This is what Canvas is built for.
  • DOM: Text rendering, input fields, scrollable lists, accessibility, tooltips. React is built for this.
  • The HUD spec (18-20px minimum fonts, 2px borders, Trello-weight cards) is much easier to build with Tailwind CSS than hand-rendered Canvas text.

Performance Considerations

What kills Canvas performance:

  • getImageData() / putImageData() on every frame (GPU readback is slow)
  • Too many drawImage() calls with different source images (texture swaps)
  • Drawing off-screen objects (no built-in culling)
  • Creating new Image objects during the render loop

What keeps it fast:

  • Sprite sheets (fewer textures)
  • Frustum culling (skip drawing objects outside the camera view)
  • Dirty rectangle optimization (only redraw changed regions)
  • Object pooling for particles/effects

Frustum Culling (Skip Off-Screen Rooms)

function isVisible(
  worldX: number,
  worldY: number,
  width: number,
  height: number,
  camera: Camera,
  canvasWidth: number,
  canvasHeight: number
): boolean {
  // Transform world coords to screen coords
  const screenX = (worldX - camera.x) * camera.zoom + canvasWidth / 2;
  const screenY = (worldY - camera.y) * camera.zoom + canvasHeight / 2;
  const screenW = width * camera.zoom;
  const screenH = height * camera.zoom;

  // Check if the bounding box intersects the viewport
  return (
    screenX + screenW > 0 &&
    screenX < canvasWidth &&
    screenY + screenH > 0 &&
    screenY < canvasHeight
  );
}

At zoom level 3, most rooms are off-screen. Culling them saves 70-80% of draw calls.

Summary: What Bobby Builds, In Order

  1. React component with useRef canvas + requestAnimationFrame loop. No re-renders driving the game.
  2. Camera system with setTransform. Pan, zoom, smooth transitions matching the room zoom spec.
  3. Sprite sheet loader. One sheet per agent, frame-based animation with elapsed-time timing.
  4. Y-sort renderer. Draw rooms back-to-front, furniture and characters sorted within each room.
  5. AABB hit detection. Convert screen clicks to world coords, test against room/agent bounding boxes.
  6. Hybrid DOM overlay. HUD, chat, menus stay in React/Tailwind. Canvas handles the game world only.
